evidenceInspected.disclosure: Variant definitions and existing editorial captions were visible during inspection. Judgment is independent but this was not a blinded review. Full batch statistics and full-match clips were not evaluated.

observations.facts: Blue has a more legible outlined preparation ring in B at 8.6/8.9; by 9.0 a projectile is visible in both. At 9.3 red has 80 HP in both and B adds a white mark on red. Logs put blue release at 8.967 and damage at 9.25.
observations.interpretation: B makes a useful distinction between getting a shot ready and confirming contact. The visible shot already communicates travel in A; the improvement is additional phase information, not a wholly new readable attack.

observations.facts: B shows red preparing near blue at 9.6, then a small release cue at 9.7 without a white damage mark; blue remains 34 HP. Later frames show blue at 12 HP and then dead with a white mark at the finishing position in B. Logs distinguish red release without damage at 9.633 from damaging melee at 11.433 and 12.217.
observations.interpretation: The missed swing is the strongest useful test: an action occurred without a successful hit. B helps avoid equating every effect with success. But even with B, the stills do not explain why that swing missed or prove that I would read the pressure reversal at normal playback speed.

observations.facts: Both panels retain red/green contact, yellow projectiles, and blue firing. B puts a white mark near green after green dies and on red after yellow damage; later small marks appear around the red/yellow contact. At 7.3 the remote ice impact has no matching hit mark. Logs record green dying at 6.983, empty ice at 7.233 and yellow damage to red at 7.567/7.600.
observations.interpretation: B makes the recipient of damage easier to locate while preserving the intersecting engagement. It does not independently identify the attacker: yellow projectiles and red melee still need to be followed. A white cross should be described as damage happened here, never as proof of who had initiative or why a dodge failed.

observations.facts: B outlines green and yellow preparation at 0.5 and shows small release accents around the rapid-fire sequence. By 1.1 red has a prominent white mark; green later loses HP while the right-hand projectile chain continues. At 2.4 the ice has landed away from fighters without a white impact cross there. Logs record multiple spread hits on red within 0.983–1.017, melee damage to green at 1.367/2.167, and zero-hit ice at 2.317.
observations.interpretation: This contrary case shows the information is compact enough that bodies/projectiles remain visible in these samples. Still, the floor has charge rings, a large ice warning, tiny release rings and projectile trails together. Their priority is weak at this scale; I can understand damage more readily than which threat deserves my next look. Multiple simultaneous damage crosses should not be counted visually as distinct causally traced attacks.

rankedConcerns.concern: Initiative remains difficult to read when multiple fighters act. Confirming a victim is easier than seeing who controls space or what escape is available.
rankedConcerns.severity: Material limit on the claim; not a blocker to comparing these alternatives.

rankedConcerns.concern: Preparation and release cues are small at the supplied two-panel scale; the ring outlines are clearer than their exact progression or directional detail.
rankedConcerns.severity: Needs owner judgment in motion; do not claim anticipation solved.

rankedConcerns.concern: Hit confirmation establishes actual damage but not attacker/projectile lineage or the reason an attack missed. Empty explosions and absent hit marks require careful wording.

tentativePreference.reason: The confirmed-hit versus released-but-missed distinction is useful. I do not see enough evidence that the extra ring/pointer detail substantially improves pressure reading.

uncertainty: Only 22 sampled paired frames were inspected, not continuous video. Timing feel, tension, animation quality and normal-speed perceptual load remain inconclusive.
Three curated local windows support a narrow presentation comparison; neither all seed behavior nor whole-match readability was assessed.
Preparation tells do not establish cancellability, punish windows or tactical commitment rules. No gameplay changes occurred between alternatives.
No unique projectile lineage was reconstructed. Logs corroborate damage/empty AOE events but cannot establish visual pleasure.
overallVerdict: Tentatively prefer B for knowing a hit really happened. Its benefit to anticipation is modest in these samples, and reading initiative in four-way fights remains unresolved. Ready for a bounded owner comparison with those limits stated.

displaySummary.title: Hits are clearer; pressure is still hard to read
displaySummary.text: B helps separate a missed swing from a real hit. In the crowded fight I still have to trace shots to know who is pressuring whom, and the preparation detail is small. Slight preference for B, based on sampled stills rather than continuous viewing.
